title: A Reproducible Synthetic Benchmark and Deterministic Validator for Evaluating LLM‑Driven NetOps: A Paired Confirmatory Comparison of a GVR Pipeline and Single‑Pass Generation
abstract: We designed, preregistered, and executed a sealed, machine‑checkable synthetic benchmark and deterministic validator to compare a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline against a frozen single‑pass LLM on operational intent→configuration tasks. The preregistered paired design used N=300 tasks across four intent categories (75 per cluster) and declared model gpt-5-mini; validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0). We used a shared‑initial generation: baseline and guarded conditions received the same initial candidate; the guarded pipeline could invoke repair only when the validator failed (≤1 repair call per task). Provider accounting recorded 300 shared initial generation calls and exactly 1 repair invocation (model_calls_used = 301). Results: baseline 299/300 passes, guarded 300/300 passes; contingency n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; paired difference = 0.0033333333333332993; paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The preregistered hypothesis that GVR produces a materially higher pass rate (target effect 0.10 at ≈80% power with N=300) was not supported. The null outcome is attributable to a near‑ceiling baseline (299/300) and minimal GVR engagement (one repair invocation). The archived execution bundle (execution/raw_results.jsonl; sha256: 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d) contains the single discordant episode identifier and the single repair provider trace; model configuration for deterministic reproduction is archived as execution/model_configuration.json (sha256: a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820). We analyse ceiling effects, provide artifact‑grounded recommendations for benchmark design, and release the full preregistration and execution artifacts for community reuse.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation, change planning, and automated remediation. Prior work demonstrates both promise and risk: LLMs can draft device configurations but produce syntax, topology, or semantic errors unless combined with verification and human oversight. The NetOps community lacks standardized, machine‑checkable benchmarks that couple operational intent tasks with deterministic validator semantics and sealed preregistration to support confirmatory comparisons of defended pipelines (generate–validate–repair, GVR) versus single‑pass generation.

This study (preregistration ac-2026-003-prereg-v1) asks a tightly specified confirmatory question: under fixed seeds and a constrained repair budget (≤1 repair call per task), does a guarded GVR pipeline materially increase the per‑task deterministic validator pass rate relative to a frozen single‑pass generator on N=300 paired intent→configuration tasks? The experimental design enforces a shared‑initial generation per task so that any guarded improvement must derive from an invoked repair rather than generation variability. We report the sealed preregistration, deterministic validator semantics, complete execution accounting, and paired confirmatory analysis, and we archive all provider traces and per‑task validator diagnostics to enable reproducibility and follow‑on benchmarking.
sections.related_work: Recent surveys and focused studies document accelerating interest in LLMs for NetOps while highlighting evaluation and safety gaps [https://openalex.org/W4406137434, https://openalex.org/W4415071524, https://openalex.org/W4402742293]. Prior empirical work shows verifier‑assisted and repair‑oriented architectures can reduce misconfigurations in limited settings [https://openalex.org/W4404652946, 10.1145/3626111.3628194], but these typically evaluate on small testbeds or require human adjudication. Complementary literature documents prompt injection, jailbreaks, hallucination, and adversarial prompt attacks as concrete operational risks for LLM‑driven NetOps [https://openalex.org/W4405181600, https://openalex.org/W4388886073]. Our contribution is an artifact‑grounded, preregistered, paired confirmatory comparison using a deterministic snapshot validator and a shared‑initial generation semantics to isolate automated repair value under a constrained budget.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and study selection. The study was preregistered as ac-2026-003-prereg-v1 and frozen before execution. Primary hypothesis H1: the GVR pipeline yields a higher per‑task validator pass rate than a frozen single‑pass generator on N=300 paired tasks (two‑sided α=0.05). The preregistration fixed task composition, validator semantics, model/adaptor configuration, exclusion rules, missingness treatments, and the analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1).

Task bank and semantics. A deterministic task generator produced N=300 synthetic intent→configuration tasks partitioned into four intent clusters (reachability, isolation, ACLs, route policies; 75 tasks each). Each task encodes initial_state, expected_final_state, allowed_fields, workflow_policies (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields, final_group_constraints), and an explicit required_sequence of ordered field changes. Tasks vary device counts (3–50) and abstract multi‑vendor device models; all tasks are synthetic and contain no private customer data. Representative per‑task payloads and reference answers appear in the archived manifest and scoring JSONs (examples and hashes are included in the execution bundle).

Validator and scoring semantics. deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version v5.0) implements the scoring rule full_intent_constraint_validation. The validator is deterministic and stateless: it performs snapshot checks that (a) parse the candidate configuration, (b) compute the implied final_state, (c) verify that required_sequence ordering and workflow_policies are satisfied, and (d) enumerate violation codes when constraints fail. The validator returns a binary VALID_CONFIGURATION pass/fail decision together with structured diagnostics (normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_codes). This strict snapshot semantics intentionally isolates syntactic/semantic correctness against declared intent constraints.

Shared‑initial generation and guarded repair semantics. To tightly control generator variance, the pipeline issued one shared initial generation per task; that shared candidate served as the baseline single‑pass output. For the guarded GVR condition the pipeline ran the deterministic validator on the same shared candidate and invoked repair only if the validator returned failure; the preregistered repair budget allowed at most one automated repair call per task (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). Planned_episode_count = 600 (300 shared initial + up to 300 repairs); stopping rules required at least 270 completed pairs. Provider_call_audit recorded stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 1}, confirming that a single repair invocation occurred during the run.

Model and runtime configuration. The declared and archived model configuration used: declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini"; requested_model = "gpt-5-mini"; provider = "openai_responses"; max_output_tokens = 2000; maximum_attempts_per_call = 1; reasoning_effort = "minimal"; store = false; temperature = null. The hosted adapter (hosted_netops_gvr_v1) operated in deterministic sampling mode as recorded in execution/model_configuration.json (sha256: a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820). In practice this means the adapter omitted stochastic sampling parameters (temperature unspecified) and relied on provider‑level deterministic invocation semantics; bit‑for‑bit reproduction therefore requires replaying archived provider call traces as recorded in execution/raw_results.jsonl (sha256: 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d).

Analysis plan. The primary estimand was paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline computed on N=300 paired binary outcomes. The preregistered test was exact McNemar two‑sided; we also computed a paired bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). Predefined sensitivity treatments for missingness and exclusions were specified; none were triggered in the run.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The execution completed per preregistration: planned_episode_count = 600, completed_episode_count = 600, complete_pair_count = 300, failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 301. Provider_call_audit confirms stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 1} and condition_counts = {shared: 300, guarded: 1} (deterministic_reconciliation). All per‑call provider traces, the single repair provider trace, and per‑task validator diagnostics are archived in the execution bundle (execution/raw_results.jsonl; sha256: 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d).

Primary confirmatory outcomes. Aggregated counts: baseline_success_count = 299/300 (baseline_success_rate = 0.9966666666666667); guarded_success_count = 300/300 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table is: n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0033333333333332993. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI (percentile, 10,000 resamples, seed 1729): [0.00, 0.01]. These aggregated artifacts appear in analysis/condition_summary.csv (sha256: 55eacb88c64f29dc9c5ce1ca7079eca9b4a94b5d3a2970dae019a81a1decf73b) and analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (sha256: 3421adb52d5791a979397368165fc2062e6b9a4a771ce49c0bcac80b02215d55).

Discordant episode and repair trace indexing. The run produced one discordant pair (baseline fail, guarded pass). The identifier of that discordant episode and the SHA‑256 of the single repair provider trace are recorded in the archived raw results; auditors can locate them in execution/raw_results.jsonl (sha256: 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d). For reproducible audit we also provide the model configuration checksum (execution/model_configuration.json sha256: a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820) and the preregistration checksum (preregistration sha256: a05938dad3a61e1f4aae518bcb42244009b0403a18387ceeff4be1d86ce87765). The single repair provider trace and the discordant episode identifier are authoritative only in the archived raw_results manifest; we do not reproduce the raw JSON line here to avoid printing per‑call provider payloads in the manuscript.

Diagnostic interpretation. Two facts explain the null confirmatory outcome. First, the baseline was near ceiling (299/300), leaving effectively no room to detect the preregistered target effect (0.10). Second, the guarded pipeline rarely differed from baseline because the validator accepted the shared candidate in almost all tasks; only one repair invocation occurred. The McNemar exact p = 1.0 follows directly from the discordant counts (n10 = 1, n01 = 0): with a single discordant in one direction, the two‑sided enumeration yields no evidence against equality under the exact test, particularly when totals are so small relative to the planned detectable effect. Numerically, given the observed contingency the maximum achievable paired improvement is 0.00333, far below the preregistered target of 0.10; this arithmetic observation explains the absence of statistical significance.
sections.discussion:
Ceiling‑effect diagnosis and implications. The preregistered design targeted detection of a 0.10 absolute paired improvement with N=300. That design assumed substantially lower baseline pass rates; the observed baseline ≈0.997 invalidates the detectability assumption. Because the guarded repair stage executed only once (provider accounting: repair = 1), the experiment principally tested whether automatic repair can correct the very small set of initial failures produced by our deterministic generator—and that set contained a single failure. Consequently, the run provides precise evidence about the specific pipeline configuration (shared‑initial generation, deterministic sampling, conservative single repair call) but not about GVR benefits under alternative, higher‑failure regimes.

Concrete benchmark design recommendations (artifact‑grounded). The execution manifest and per‑task diagnostics directly motivate practical changes for future benchmarks aimed at evaluating repair value: (A) increase baseline task difficulty or inject adversarial seed modes so that initial generation failures are common enough for repair to exercise (the archived difficulty labels and validation_before/after diagnostics show many tasks are labeled "medium" or "hard" yet the generator succeeded, suggesting generator/task mismatch); (B) permit iterative repair budgets (multiple repair attempts per failed candidate) so localized, multi‑step corrective reasoning can be evaluated; (C) evaluate multiple independent generations per task as baseline samples rather than a single shared candidate to measure generator variance and selection‑by‑repair effects; (D) consider stateful or emulative validators that model runtime temporal dynamics (not just snapshot checks) to expose ordering and in‑flight side‑effect failures. Each recommendation derives from execution accounting (300 shared initial generations, repair=1) and archived per‑task validator traces that identify which workflow patterns (e.g., shutdown_configure_restore, make_before_break_uplink_switchover) were easiest or hardest for the generator.

External validity and scope. Our synthetic tasks abstract multi‑vendor device models and snapshot validators; they do not capture vendor CLI idiosyncrasies, transient runtime effects, or production heterogeneity. Only gpt-5-mini was declared and evaluated. Thus, conclusions are narrowly scoped: the GVR pipeline did not produce a materially higher pass rate than the frozen single‑pass generator under the chosen, preregistered pipeline, task bank, deterministic sampling mode, and repair budget. The archived artifacts nevertheless enable community extensions (harder tasks, multi‑generation baselines, iterative repair budgets, multi‑model comparisons) without reconstructing the original pipeline.
sections.conclusion:
We preregistered, executed, and archived a sealed synthetic NetOps benchmark and deterministic validator and ran a paired confirmatory comparison of a guarded GVR pipeline versus a frozen single‑pass gpt-5-mini generator on N=300 intent→configuration tasks. Both approaches achieved near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300; guarded 300/300). The preregistered hypothesis that GVR materially improves pass rate (target 0.10) was not supported on this task set. Provider accounting shows the guarded repair stage executed only once across N=300 tasks (shared_initial_generation=300, repair=1), so the guarded condition rarely differed from baseline; this pipeline inactivity constrains claims about repair effectiveness. We release the preregistration (sha256: a05938dad3a61e1f4aae518bcb42244009b0403a18387ceeff4be1d86ce87765), execution manifest, raw responses (execution/raw_results.jsonl; sha256: 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d), per‑task validator traces, and analysis artifacts to support community extensions that target regimes where repair can be exercised and measured reliably.

Data and artifact pointers. Authoritative execution artifacts cited in this paper are archived in the bundled execution manifest: execution/model_configuration.json (sha256: a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820), execution/raw_results.jsonl (sha256: 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d), analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (sha256: 3421adb52d5791a979397368165fc2062e6b9a4a771ce49c0bcac80b02215d55), analysis/condition_summary.csv (sha256: 55eacb88c64f29dc9c5ce1ca7079eca9b4a94b5d3a2970dae019a81a1decf73b), and the preregistration artifact (sha256: a05938dad3a61e1f4aae518bcb42244009b0403a18387ceeff4be1d86ce87765). The single discordant episode identifier and the single repair provider trace are recorded inside execution/raw_results.jsonl (sha256: 0d841d29...). Reproducers should consult those artifacts and the archived provider call traces for exact replay or audit.

limitations: Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces snapshot intent constraints but does not model temporal in‑flight execution dynamics, vendor CLI idiosyncrasies, or asynchronous side effects.

External validity: tasks are synthetic (device counts 3–50, abstracted multi‑vendor models) and may not capture production heterogeneity; findings do not imply equivalent performance on real production networks or private customer data.

Ceiling effect: near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300, guarded 300/300) reduce sensitivity to detect the preregistered target effect (0.10) and therefore constrain confirmatory inference about practical superiority of GVR under broader conditions.
Model and scope limits: only gpt-5-mini was declared and evaluated; findings do not generalize to other model families or sizes without further experiments.

GVR engagement: the guarded repair stage executed only once across N=300 tasks (provider recorded stage_counts: shared_initial_generation=300, repair=1), so the guarded condition rarely differed from baseline; this pipeline inactivity constrains conclusions about repair effectiveness under alternative trigger policies or larger repair budgets.
Failure‑mode analysis: only one discordant outcome occurred (n10=1), leaving exploratory failure clustering and subgroup inference underpowered and inconclusive.

Reproducibility caveat: reproducing identical hosted model outputs may require access to the same hosted model release and provider invocation semantics recorded in the archived model configuration and the per‑call provider traces archived in the execution bundle.

Artifact‑inclusion note: the exact per‑task artifacts that contain the single repair provider trace and the single discordant episode identifier are present in the archived execution bundle (execution/raw_results.jsonl; sha256: 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d) and are authoritative for auditors.
